claims.text: The material consists of sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt quinary high-entropy alloy nanoparticles deposited on a silicon nitride membrane by pulsed laser deposition.
The as-deposited nanoparticles initially have an FCC structure.
The initial elemental distribution is homogeneous.
The initial particles have elliptical or other non-equilibrium shapes, potentially related to icosahedral or truncated-octahedral precursors.
Heating produces surface segregation and evaporation of Au and Cu.
Surface-energy minimization gradients override sluggish diffusion in these nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism becomes dominant above a critical temperature at which surface-diffusion activation barriers are overcome.
The high surface-to-volume ratio creates surface-energy anisotropy and local chemical-potential gradients.
These gradients provide a surface-diffusion driving force independent of bulk configurational entropy.
Au and Cu have sufficiently unfavorable surface energetics relative to the matrix to drive their migration to the particle surface.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu creates concentration gradients that facilitate their evaporation.
Reduced surface-diffusion barriers permit rapid atomic transport despite constraints on bulk diffusion.
Selective elemental loss can occur in a high-entropy alloy at elevated temperature despite expectations based on high entropy or sluggish diffusion.
Surface diffusion and elemental loss cause particle shrinkage and rounding from elliptical or icosahedral shapes toward spherical geometries.
The remaining particle cores will exhibit a narrower size distribution after Au and Cu loss.
The onset of accelerated shape change will coincide with significant surface diffusion rather than bulk diffusion.
The mechanism applies only to particles smaller than 10 nm because surface-energy terms dominate their Gibbs free energy.
The mechanism should fail in particles larger than 50 nm or in bulk material, where bulk entropy effects dominate.
Particles will be heated from ambient temperature to above 800 K while morphology and composition are monitored in real time.
Comparing 3 nm and 15 nm particles with icosahedral and truncated-octahedral initial shapes can test whether reshaping follows surface-energy anisotropy.

contradictions.description: The query reports a widening particle-size distribution during heating, whereas the predicted outcome states that the remaining cores will have a narrowing size distribution.
